title: Human-rights training was a formal security-assistance requirement before its provision and effectiveness were systematically tracked
source_unit: Department of Defense and Department of State human-rights training oversight and monitoring systems for foreign security forces
geography: United States security-assistance system and foreign security-force training programs

observations.period: GAO-19-554 published August 2019; DOD and State implementation follow-up through 2021

denominator.unit: human-rights training activities and funding records across DOD and State programs; aggregate universe not disclosed

initial_tracking.value: DOD did not systematically track mandated human-rights training, leaving only limited information on provision and funding; State relied on DOD for military-force tracking

initial_effectiveness_evaluation.value: DOD and State had not evaluated the effectiveness of human-rights training for foreign security forces

dod_tracking_followup.value: new security-cooperation tracking system fields and quarterly Section 333 reports included human-rights training status by 2020

dod_evaluation_followup.value: DOD integrated human-rights elements into pre-design assessments and established a post-activity evaluation timeline by 2021

state_evaluation_followup.value: State transmitted an IMET monitoring and evaluation plan to Congress in 2020 with human-rights objectives and indicators

observations.method: GAO review of laws, regulations, agency training and funding data, course catalogs, and interviews with DOD and State officials; follow-up status is taken from GAO's recommendation records rather than an independent outcome evaluation of trainees.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not measure what trainees learned, whether training changed conduct, civilian protection, partner legitimacy, abuse rates, or external behavior. Tracking and evaluation reforms establish administrative capacity, not human-rights outcomes. The programs and populations are heterogeneous and the aggregate activity denominator is not reported.
observations.subgroup: Foreign security-force trainees receiving DOD- or State-supported human-rights or international humanitarian-law content; Section 333 and IMET routes are discussed separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: A formal training requirement may coexist with effective local practice even before centralized tracking, while a new tracking field may improve visibility without improving conduct. Conversely, weak initial oversight can conceal both successful and unsuccessful training rather than prove either.

related_sources.claim: GAO's Section 333 delivery and evaluation review supplies a separate capability and reliability stage
GAO's Section 333 planning review supplies a separate absorptive-capacity and sustainment stage

boundary: This record adds a rights-legitimacy and oversight layer to security assistance: formal training, tracking, and evaluation can lag the provision of equipment and capacity-building. It does not establish trainee learning, rights compliance, civilian protection, partner legitimacy, or strategic success.
